newsitem.title: USA: Stocks rebound, bonds unchanged, dollar falls.
newsitem.headline: Stocks rebound, bonds unchanged, dollar falls.

text.p: Stocks rebounded Thursday, with the Nasdaq index chalking up its sixth record close in a row as investors cheered upbeat corporate earnings.
Bonds were barely changed.
The dollar fell from a 3-1/2-year high against the mark after Germany's top central banker said he believed the dollar has made a full recovery from its all-time lows in 1995.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended up 44.33 points at 7,886.76 after Wednesday's 120-point loss.
The Nasdaq Composite index gained 4.30 points to 1,490.93.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,764 to 1,038 on heavy volume of 551 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
Blue chips were again buoyed by solid earnings news, this time from General Electric Co., which reported a record profit of $2.16 billion in the second quarter. GE climbed 1-1/16 to 69-1/2.
The early earnings returns, particularly from blue-chip companies, fuelled optimism about the quarter.

"Most of the negative feelings that existed coming into this quarter seemed to centre on fears of higher interest rates and the impact of a too-strong dollar," said Robert Froehlich, chief investment strategist at Kemper Funds. "Neither of those really developed."

Technology stocks continued their torrid streak, overcoming a weak showing by computer chip bellwether Intel Corp., which fell 2-1/2 to 150-1/8 after Salomon Brothers voiced caution about the company's upcoming results.
Investors opted to focus on the bigger picture, however, looking past Intel's problems, which largely involve issues related to its transition to a new generation of chips.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was unchanged, with a yield of 6.56 percent.
The dollar fell nearly 2 pfennigs after extending this week's string of powerful gains in Tokyo trading to 1.7665 marks, a peak not seen since February 1994.
The dollar fell to 1.7510 marks from 1.7605 marks late Wednesday, but rose to 113.11 Japanese yen from 112.75 yen.
August gold futures recovered slightly, rising $1.90 to $320.80 an ounce on New York's Commodity Exchange.
Coffee prices fell after a U.S. Agriculture Department official said a surprising estimate of the crop in top grower Brazil this week by one of the department's own analysts was probably too low.
At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, coffee for September delivery closed down 15.35 cents a pound at 161.70 cents, its lowest price since April 10.
Grain prices also fell back as continued fine weather in the Midwest sparked selling by speculators.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, corn for July delivery closed down 2 cents a bushel at $2.47-3/4. July soybeans closed down 10 cents a bushel at $7.79 and July wheat closed down 4-1/4 cents a bushel at $3.21-1/2.

At the New York Mercantile Exchnage, oil prices closed mostly lower after shrugging off news that Colombian rebels had dynamited a pipeline for the second time this week and forced a halt in oil production at the large Cano Limon field.
Crude for August delivery closed down 21 cents a barrel at $19.38.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 closed at 4,767.8, up 5.4 points, or 0.11 percent. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average closed at 19,754.78, up 57.61 points, or 0.29 percent.
